name: Stats
what: Shows how many people visited each of this portfolio's product sites, where they came from, and which posts, links and sources led to signups and sales.
glance: Visitors, sources, funnel, top pages, countries and tagged links, for one site or all of them
Yesterday, the last 7 days or the last 30, each against the period before
Each one traced to the post, email or ad the buyer arrived from
A Telegram summary every morning and a week-on-week summary every Monday
archHi:
Stats is a private dashboard for this portfolio's product sites. It shows how many people visited each site, where they came from and what they did next, from App Store clicks to signups and sales. Its figures come from a tracking setup that each site gets with one command.

  1. Tag. Every post, email or ad carries a tagged link made by the tool, so a visit can be traced to what brought it.
  2. Record. Each site sends its visits and clicks to PostHog through a proxy on its own domain, with a cookie banner where the law needs one.
  3. Join. A sale arrives from the payment provider's webhook carrying the visitor's checkout data, so it lands on the same visitor, and under the same source, as the visit.
  4. Read. The dashboard shows every site together or one at a time, for yesterday, the last 7 days or the last 30. A Telegram message sums up each morning, and the whole week each Monday.

The page and the messages take every figure from the same function, so they always agree, and each sale can be followed back to the post that brought the buyer.
arch:
A Node.js server on an always-on Mac mini serves the page and a small JSON API through a Cloudflare tunnel. Figures are read from PostHog with HogQL queries and drawn in the browser by plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

  • One source of figures. The page and the daily and weekly messages both read one shared function. No figure is computed anywhere else.
  • One source per visitor. Each visitor counts under a single source: a tagged link with its campaign, a search engine, a referring site, or Direct when there is no referrer. Their clicks, checkouts and sales count under the same source, so every source shows what its visitors went on to do.
  • Two kinds of site. A site that sells shows App Store clicks, Mac downloads, buy clicks, checkouts, sales and revenue before fees. Any other site shows signups or waitlist joins, the signup rate, visitors from tagged links and pages per visit.

Each site has four views, and each opens with one sentence on what happened in the period and three highlights: the top source's share, the change in visitors and the source that converts best.

ViewShows
Overviewvisitors per day by source as an area or bar chart, the headline figures, the source mix, the funnel, top pages, countries and tagged links
Sourcesa flow from each source to what its visitors did, and the conversion rate of each source
Funneleach step from visit to sale or signup, with the drop-off at each
Linkseach tagged link with its visitors and results
  • Filtering runs in the browser. Tapping a source filters the page to it from the figures already loaded, with no new query. Top pages and countries stay unfiltered.
  • All sites at once. The all-sites view lists every site, busiest first, with its visitors, the change on the period before and a line of its daily totals. A searchable picker opens any one site.
  • Calendar days in one time zone. Yesterday, the last 7 days and the last 30 all end on the previous day in the configured zone, and each is compared with the period before.
  • Internal visits are left out. Opening a site once with ?internal=1 tags that browser internal, and its visits stay out of the figures.
  • Stale figures are labelled. Figures are cached for five minutes. When PostHog cannot be reached, the server returns the last good figures marked stale, and the page shows the time they are from.
  • Sign-in fails closed. The password exists on the server only as a PBKDF2 hash, and without a valid hash file every request is refused. Sessions are signed cookies valid for 12 hours, or 30 days when kept, and repeated misses lock an address out for a wait that doubles up to five minutes.
  • Remote requests always need a session. Anything arriving through the tunnel counts as remote, whichever local port it reaches. The PostHog key is read once at start and never appears in a response or a log line.
  • Markup is never built from data. Every value is written as text, and the page's content security policy forbids inline styles.
  • Phone and desktop. The layout follows the width of the page. On a phone the period switch moves to a bar at the bottom of the screen, and light and dark follow the system setting.
  • A sample-data address. A second address draws the same page from a seeded event history, so the dashboard can be shown without its real figures.
  • Scheduled messages. At 09:00 each site gets a block with yesterday's visitors, top sources, clicks, sales and top pages, then whether each site is still sending visits and a link to the page. At 09:10 on Mondays the week is set against the week before, with the best source and up to three next steps.
proc:
• A Node.js server, PostHog and Telegram. The tool is Node.js 22 with a single package dependency. The page is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step, reading a JSON API. Figures come from PostHog through HogQL queries. The server runs as a launchd service on an always-on Mac mini and is reached through a Cloudflare tunnel; the same machine sends the scheduled messages to Telegram.
  • A single source of truth for figures. One function computes every figure, and the dashboard, its API and both Telegram messages are views over its result.
  • Mechanism separated from policy. The engine is generic and names nothing of its owner: no products, machines, organisation or secret store. Product names, domains, wording and how keys are fetched reach it only through a config file kept in a separate personal layer.
  • Desired-state convergence. Setup compares what a site should have with what it has and writes only the difference, so a second run with the same flags changes nothing.
  • First-party collection. Tracking goes through a proxy on the site's own domain, which drops the site's cookies and authorization headers before anything reaches PostHog.
  • Money events come from the server. Sales and refunds are recorded from the payment provider's webhooks, and each payment counts once. The browser never reports a sale.
  • Fail closed, serve stale. Missing credentials lock the page for everyone. A failing upstream falls back to the last good figures, labelled with their time.
